summary_markdown: # North Carolina — Commercial UAS Regulatory Summary **Prepared for:** AEC (surveying, mapping, construction, inspection) UAS program management **Research date:** August 1, 2026 | **Version:** 2.2 (Workstream 9 retrofit — August 7, 2026) **Model / checkpoint:** Objective research and Phase 2 model/checkpoint were not recorded in this legacy state packet. **Interpretation scope:** Agent Instructions v6 (August 2, 2026) **Scope note:** Federal FAA Part 107 is the baseline for all commercial sUAS operations nationwide and is not restated here. Per current research-phase scope (Agent Instructions v6), this summary covers North Carolina **state and state-agency** UAS authorities only — local (municipal/county) ordinances and tribal rules are deferred to a later phase. North Carolina is neither a broad-preemption state (like Texas or Arizona) nor a fully open state (like Colorado or New York): local governments have a narrow, property-based authority to regulate UAS launch/recovery from land they own (Section 4 below), which somewhat narrows — but does not eliminate — the significance of that deferral. Full citations and metadata are in `NC_UAS_Source_Register.csv`. > **Status:** A first pass of source collection, objective summaries, and practical interpretation is complete for this state. Ongoing work is expanding source coverage and improving quality review and processing efficiency across the project. --- ## 1. State UAS Regulatory Overview North Carolina has one of the most extensively codified state UAS regulatory frameworks reviewed to date, built out over multiple session laws since 2014 (S.L. 2014-100, 2015-232, 2016-90, 2017-160, 2017-179, and 2023-63) and recently simplified by a significant 2024 deregulatory change. The core framework spans privacy/surveillance restrictions (§ 15A-300.1), launch/recovery site consent with a narrow local-ordinance carve-out (§ 15A-300.2), a correctional-facility buffer with a detailed commercial-operator exception (§ 15A-300.3), a newer and unusually severely penalized forest-fire buffer (§ 15A-300.4, enacted 2023), interference with manned aircraft (§ 14-280.3), weapon-attached UAS and hunting/fishing restrictions (§ 14-401.24), thermal-imaging distribution restrictions (§ 14-401.25), and wildlife-harassment-by-UAS (§ 113-295(a1)). Importantly, effective December 1, 2024, the state repealed its separate UAS knowledge-test and commercial-operator-permit requirement (formerly §§ 63-95/63-96) after a legislative veto override — commercial and government operators now need only comply with FAA Part 107, a materially favorable simplification for AEC firms operating in North Carolina. State parks independently prohibit UAV launch/landing absent a Special Activity Permit. ## 2. Statewide UAS Laws and Regulations ### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.1 — Restrictions on Use of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (Privacy/Surveillance) *Binding law | Current, enacted 2014, amended 2017* **Objective Summary:** Prohibits any person, entity, or State agency from using a UAS to conduct surveillance of a person, dwelling and curtilage, or private real property without consent, or to photograph an individual without consent for publication (with a newsgathering/public-event exception). Law enforcement and emergency-management exceptions apply. Creates a civil cause of action with $5,000 statutory damages per photograph/video, plus costs and fees; violating evidence is generally inadmissible in criminal prosecutions. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Routine aerial mapping and inspection is not the targeted conduct, but avoid incidental surveillance-style capture of neighboring private property or individuals without consent. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** This creates a private civil cause of action with statutory damages distinct from any criminal exposure — document flight purpose and project boundaries near residential areas. ### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.2 — Regulation of Launch and Recovery Sites *Binding law | Current, enacted 2014* **Objective Summary:** Prohibits launching or recovering a UAS from State or private property without consent. Separately authorizes a unit of local government to adopt an ordinance regulating UAS launch/recovery from property the local government owns — the primary statutory basis for local UAS ordinances in North Carolina, narrower than a general local police-power grant. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Obtain documented consent before launching/recovering from any State or private property outside the client's project site; check for a locally-owned-property launch/recovery ordinance if the project involves city/county land. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** This is the primary hook for North Carolina's narrower, property-based local ordinance authority — distinguish it from a broad local police-power grant for clients. ### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.3 — UAS Near a Confinement or Correctional Facility Prohibited *Binding law | Current, effective December 1, 2017* **Objective Summary:** Prohibits UAS operation within 500 ft horizontal / 250 ft vertical of a local confinement facility or State/federal correctional facility. Exceptions include written facility consent, law enforcement, and a detailed commercial/public-utility exception (150 ft horizontal/vertical buffer, 24-hour notice, qualifying business purpose, FAA and Chapter 63 Article 10 compliance, no unescorted entry). Penalties range from a Class I misdemeanor up to a Class H felony (weapon delivery) or Class I felony (contraband delivery). **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Directly relevant to infrastructure work near a North Carolina jail or prison — the narrower commercial exception (150 ft buffer + 24-hour notice) may apply to qualifying utility/infrastructure inspection work, but document each required element. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** The commercial exception's condition (d) cross-references Chapter 63, Article 10 compliance, which was substantially repealed in 2024 (see below) — confirm what that cross-reference now requires before relying on the exception. ### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.4 — UAS Near a Forest Fire Prohibited *Binding law | Current, enacted 2023* **Objective Summary:** Prohibits UAS operation within 3,000 ft horizontal or vertical of any forest fire within North Carolina Forest Service jurisdiction. Exceptions for consent from the official in charge, law enforcement, and Forest Service personnel. Penalties are severely tiered by consequence — up to a Class D felony if the violation proximately causes death, down to a Class A1 misdemeanor, each with a mandatory minimum $1,000 fine. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Directly relevant to post-wildfire damage assessment work — do not fly within 3,000 ft of an active forest fire without consent from the managing official, given the severe injury-tiered felony exposure. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** This is one of the most severely penalized state UAS statutes reviewed to date; document specific consent and warrant conservative compliance. ### N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 14-280.3, 14-401.24, 14-401.25, 113-295(a1) — Additional Criminal Code Provisions *Binding law | Current* **Objective Summary:** § 14-280.3 makes willful interference with a manned aircraft via UAS a Class H felony. § 14-401.24 makes weapon-attached UAS possession/use a Class E felony and UAS-assisted fishing/hunting a Class 1 misdemeanor. § 14-401.25 makes publishing/disseminating non-consensual thermal/infrared UAS imagery revealing interior building activity a Class A1 misdemeanor. § 113-295(a1) makes UAS-assisted wildlife-taking interference a Class 1 misdemeanor. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Weapon and hunting/fishing provisions have low relevance to standard AEC payloads; the thermal-imaging distribution restriction is directly relevant to building-envelope/energy-audit inspection work — obtain owner consent before publishing thermal deliverables revealing interior activity. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Distinguish conducting a thermal inspection (not itself prohibited) from publishing/disseminating imagery without consent (prohibited); maintain airspace deconfliction documentation given § 14-280.3's felony exposure. ## 3. State Agency UAS Requirements ### Repeal of State UAS Knowledge Test and Commercial Operator Permit *Binding law (repeal) | Effective December 1, 2024* **Objective Summary:** Session Law 2024-15 (House Bill 198, enacted via veto override) repealed Chapter 63, Article 10 (formerly §§ 63-95, 63-96), eliminating the separate North Carolina UAS knowledge test and State commercial-operator permit that had applied on top of FAA Part 107. Commercial and government operators now need only comply with FAA Part 107 or other applicable federal authorization. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Do not plan for a North Carolina State UAS permit or knowledge test — this requirement no longer exists. FAA Part 107 remains the operative licensing requirement. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Update pre-2024 compliance materials referencing the old permit/test; note the unresolved cross-reference in § 15A-300.3(b)(3)(d) to "Chapter 63, Article 10" compliance, which is now a largely repealed article. ### Parks — North Carolina Division of Parks and Recreation *Binding administrative regulation | Current, amended 2022* **Objective Summary:** 07 NCAC 13B .1204 prohibits voluntarily bringing, landing, or taking off with a UAV/drone on Division of Parks and Recreation property, except under a Special Activity or Special Use Permit (07 NCAC 13B .0104). **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Apply for a Special Activity/Special Use Permit well before any AEC UAS work planned within a state park boundary. - **Agency Practitioner:** Start with the site manager or permitting office for North Carolina Division of Parks and Recreation before scheduling fieldwork, because property-specific conditions may control the route and timing. Request the current form, lead time, fee, insurance and FAA-document checklist, and site restrictions, then keep the signed approval and conditions in the mission file. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the permit in the project file; confirm current procedure and any park-specific variations directly with the Division. ### Professional Licensing — Unlicensed-Surveying Enforcement Against Drone Mapping/Photogrammetry Operators *Binding law and binding federal appellate precedent | Current — the Fourth Circuit's ruling became final April 20, 2026* **Objective Summary:** This record was materially expanded in the August 2026 retrofit. North Carolina's licensing framework (Chapter 89C) requires PE/PLS licensees to practice only within their competency — but the real, currently binding risk is NCBELS's active enforcement pattern, not a mere gap in guidance. Since 2018, NCBELS has issued cease-and-desist letters to at least a half-dozen drone companies for practicing land surveying without a license. In the best-documented case, the Board formally warned Michael Jones (360 Virtual Drone Services LLC, Goldsboro) that his orthomosaic mapping, thermal imaging, and geospatial-metadata photography constituted unlicensed surveying — regardless of whether he claimed to establish legal boundaries. Jones sued on First Amendment grounds; the Fourth Circuit ruled for NCBELS on May 20, 2024 (*360 Virtual Drone Services LLC v. Ritter*, 102 F.4th 263), applying a "loosened" First Amendment standard to occupational speech and upholding the Board's authority to restrict non-licensees' communication of maps and 3D digital models. The U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari on April 20, 2026, making the ruling final. Per NCBELS's stated enforcement position, providing a client with aerial photography containing geospatial metadata or coordinate/distance data, an orthomosaic map, a 3D digital model from photogrammetry, an elevation/topographic product, or rough distance/volume measurements from processed aerial imagery all risk unlicensed-practice enforcement absent a PE/PLS license. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Treat any UAS-derived deliverable containing geospatial metadata, coordinates, distances, elevations, volumes, or an orthomosaic/3D model as presumptively within NCBELS's asserted licensing scope. Route such deliverables through a licensed North Carolina PE or PLS regardless of whether the product purports to establish legal boundaries — a disclaimer does not avoid the licensing requirement under NCBELS's enforcement position. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Advise clients this is an active, currently enforced, and now judicially settled risk, not a hypothetical gap. Confirm licensure status before a non-licensed operator delivers any mapping/photogrammetry product with the characteristics NCBELS has targeted; a First Amendment defense is foreclosed in this Circuit following the final Fourth Circuit ruling. ## 4. State/Local Regulatory Boundary **Objective Summary:** North Carolina occupies a middle position: § 15A-300.2(b) gives local governments narrow authority to regulate UAS launch/recovery from property they own (city/county parks, facilities), but does not grant a broad power to regulate UAS operation generally within their jurisdiction. Municipal examples located include Raleigh's and Wake Forest's park-specific UAS guidelines. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Treat local-ordinance risk as concentrated on locally owned property rather than a broad citywide patchwork; confirm whether a project site is on locally owned park/government land. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** A property-specific municipal-ordinance check remains warranted in a later research phase, particularly for city/county park land. ## 5. Unresolved Operational Questions - **Chapter 63, Article 10 cross-reference:** § 15A-300.3(b)(3)(d)'s commercial correctional-facility exception requires compliance with "Chapter 63, Article 10," which was substantially repealed effective Dec. 1, 2024 — confirm with NCDOT's Division of Aviation how this condition now operates. - **Local ordinances:** Out of scope for this phase; North Carolina's narrow property-based local authority (Section 4) still warrants a project-specific check for locally owned land. - **Jockey's Ridge State Park:** Secondary sources note a historically separate operator-permit arrangement for this park's unique dune-launch activity; not independently verified in this pass. - **Professional licensing enforcement scope:** NCBELS's exact current published enforcement/guidance position (21 NCAC 56) for specific deliverable characteristics (e.g., where the line falls between a simple aerial photograph and a metadata-tagged "mapping" product) was not independently re-verified section-by-section in this pass — confirm directly with the Board or NC counsel for a specific engagement. ## 6. Confidence Summary | Finding | Confidence | |---|---| | § 15A-300.1 (privacy/surveillance) | High — verified directly against the NC General Assembly's official codified statutes | | § 15A-300.2 (launch/recovery sites; local authority) | High — verified directly against NCDOT's official summary document | | § 15A-300.3 (correctional facility buffer) | High — verified directly against NCDOT's official summary document | | § 15A-300.4 (forest fire buffer) | High — verified directly against the NC General Assembly's official codified statutes | | §§ 14-280.3, 14-401.24, 14-401.25, 113-295(a1) | High — verified directly against NCDOT's official summary document | | Repeal of §§ 63-95/63-96 (permit/test) | High — verified directly against NCDOT's own current webpage, corroborated by industry news | | 07 NCAC 13B .1204 (state park UAS prohibition) | High — verified directly against the NC Office of Administrative Hearings' official NCAC database | | Narrow local-authority characterization | Moderate — research result, not a comprehensive local-ordinance survey | | NCBELS unlicensed-surveying enforcement (Chapter 89C + *360 Virtual Drone Services LLC v. Ritter*) | High — enforcement pattern and Fourth Circuit ruling verified directly via the Institute for Justice's case page (counsel of record) and cross-checked against Justia's reproduction of the published opinion (102 F.4th 263) | *This document is objective legal/regulatory summary plus labeled practical interpretation. It is not legal advice; consult North Carolina counsel for project-specific compliance determinations. Local ordinances and tribal UAS considerations are out of scope for this phase per current research instructions.*

records.uas_topic: Privacy / unauthorized surveillance and photography by UAS
records.regulated_party: Any person, entity, or State agency
records.regulated_activity: Conducting surveillance of a person/dwelling/curtilage or private real property without consent; photographing an individual without consent for publication/public dissemination
records.requirement_type: Prohibition, with law-enforcement and emergency-management exceptions
records.summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.1(b) prohibits any person, entity, or State agency from using a UAS to (1) conduct surveillance of a person or a dwelling and its curtilage without consent, or of private real property without the owner's/easement holder's/lessee's consent, or (2) photograph an individual without consent for the purpose of publishing or publicly disseminating the photograph (with an exception for newsgathering, newsworthy events, or events/places open to the general public). Law enforcement agencies have five listed exceptions (subsection (c)), including counter-terrorism determinations, plain-view surveillance, search warrants, exigent circumstances, and photographing public gatherings; an emergency management agency exception (subsection (c1)) covers incident command, reconnaissance, search and rescue, damage assessment, hazard risk management, and floodplain mapping. A person whose privacy is violated has a civil cause of action with statutory damages of $5,000 per photograph/video, plus costs and attorney's fees (subsection (e)); evidence obtained in violation is generally inadmissible in criminal prosecutions (subsection (f)).
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Routine AEC aerial mapping, inspection, and construction-progress photography over a project site is not the conduct this statute targets, but avoid incidental surveillance-style capture of neighboring private property, dwellings, or individuals without consent — adjust flight paths or camera settings near residential areas bordering a project site.
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This statute creates a private civil cause of action with statutory damages ($5,000 per image/video) distinct from any criminal exposure — document the professional/survey purpose and project boundary of any flight near residential property, and obtain consent where the flight path may reasonably capture private property or individuals outside the project scope.

records.source_title: Use of an Unmanned Aircraft System Near a Confinement or Correctional Facility Prohibited
records.regulated_party: Any person, entity, or State agency
records.regulated_activity: Operating a UAS within 500 ft horizontal / 250 ft vertical of a local confinement facility or State/federal correctional facility
records.requirement_type: Prohibition, with a written-consent defense and a narrower commercial/public-utility exception
records.permit_or_approval_required: No — but a narrower distance/notice regime applies to public utilities and commercial entities (see summary)
records.public_agency_only: Yes, for public utilities/providers/commercial entities meeting the statutory conditions
records.summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.3(a) prohibits operating a UAS within a horizontal distance of 500 ft or vertical distance of 250 ft from any local confinement facility (as defined in G.S. 153A-217) or State/federal correctional facility, measured outward from the facility's exterior walls, perimeter fences, or a marked boundary with notices posted no more than 100 yards apart. Subsection (b) provides exceptions for: (1) a person with written consent from the official in responsible charge of the facility; (2) a law enforcement officer acting under § 15A-300.1(c); and (3) a public utility, § 146-29(a)(6) provider, or commercial entity that (a) stays outside a narrower 150 ft horizontal/150 ft vertical buffer, (b) gives the facility's responsible official at least 24 hours' notice (commercial entities compliant with § 15A-300.1 are exempt from this notice requirement), (c) uses the UAS for utility/provider infrastructure inspection or other business purposes, (d) operates for commercial purposes in compliance with FAA rules and Chapter 63, Article 10, and (e) does not physically enter the prohibited space without a facility escort. Emergency management agencies, EMS, firefighters, and law enforcement are exempt when responding to an emergency. Penalties range from a Class I misdemeanor ($500 fine) for a bare violation, up to a Class H felony ($1,500 fine) for delivering or attempting to deliver a weapon, or a Class I felony ($1,000 fine) for delivering or attempting to deliver contraband. Violating UAS are subject to law-enforcement seizure and forfeiture.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This is directly relevant to any AEC infrastructure-inspection or mapping work near a North Carolina jail or prison — a commercial AEC operator inspecting nearby utility infrastructure may be able to use the narrower 150 ft/150 ft commercial exception (with 24-hour notice) rather than needing outright facility consent, but confirm the exact facility boundary and posted-notice markings on site, and document FAA Part 107 compliance since that is a condition of the commercial exception.
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Do not assume general FAA Part 107 certification alone satisfies this statute — the commercial exception requires meeting all five listed conditions (150 ft buffer, 24-hour notice or § 15A-300.1 compliance, qualifying business purpose, FAA/Chapter 63 Article 10 compliance, and no unescorted entry); document each element given the felony exposure tied to weapon/contraband delivery, and note that Chapter 63, Article 10 (referenced in condition (d)) was substantially repealed effective Dec. 1, 2024 (see NC-009) — confirm what compliance with 'Article 10' now requires in light of that repeal.
records.verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against NCDOT's official summary document, which reproduces the statute word-for-word from the ratified act (S.L. 2017-179); note the statute's own commercial-exception condition (d) cross-references Chapter 63, Article 10, which was substantially repealed in 2024 — see NC-009 for that unresolved interaction.
records.notes: High-priority item: confirm with NCDOT's Division of Aviation how the 2024 repeal of Chapter 63, Article 10's permit/test requirements affects the 'compliance with Article 10' condition in § 15A-300.3(b)(3)(d), since that cross-reference may now point to a largely repealed article.

news.headline: Drones carrying contraband into NC prisons on the rise, officials say
news.relevance_note: Directly on-topic for NC-003's confinement/correctional-facility UAS prohibition: reports NC Department of Adult Correction Secretary Leslie Dismukes confirming rising drone-borne contraband deliveries statewide, a June 2026 Columbus County arrest of four people tied to a drone drug-delivery plot at Columbus Correctional Institution, and NCDAC's active work with the FAA on drone-mitigation rules for state prisons -- the exact enforcement gap (no counter-drone authority yet) and regulated activity NC-003 addresses.

records.regulated_party: Any person, entity, or State agency
records.regulated_activity: Operating a UAS within 3,000 ft horizontal or vertical distance of any forest fire within North Carolina Forest Service jurisdiction
records.requirement_type: Prohibition, with consent, law-enforcement, and Forest Service exceptions
records.summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.4(a), enacted in 2023, prohibits operating a UAS within a horizontal or vertical distance of 3,000 ft from any forest fire within North Carolina Forest Service jurisdiction, measured outward from the fire's or fire-control lines' furthest exterior perimeter. Exceptions (subsection (b)) apply to a person with consent from the official in responsible charge of the fire, a law enforcement officer acting under § 15A-300.1(c), and Forest Service employees/those acting under their direction. Penalties are unusually severe and tiered by consequence: up to a Class D felony if the violation proximately causes another person's death, down to a Class A1 misdemeanor for a violation not otherwise covered, each carrying a mandatory minimum $1,000 fine; a Class G or H felony applies specifically where the violation interferes with emergency operations. Violating UAS are subject to law-enforcement seizure and forfeiture.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This statute is directly relevant to any AEC post-wildfire damage assessment or infrastructure-inspection work — do not fly within 3,000 ft of an active forest fire without first obtaining consent from the official in charge of managing that fire, given the unusually severe, injury-tiered felony exposure (up to Class D felony if death results).
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the specific consent obtained from the Forest Service or incident-command official before any flight near an active or recently active forest fire; this is one of the most severely penalized state UAS statutes reviewed to date and warrants conservative compliance given the felony exposure tied to interference with emergency operations even absent injury.

records.source_title: Unlawful Harassment of Persons Taking Wildlife Resources (UAS-specific provision)
records.regulated_activity: Using a UAS to interfere with the lawful taking of wildlife resources, or to drive, harass, or intentionally disturb wildlife resources for the purpose of disrupting lawful taking
records.summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 113-295(a1) makes it a Class 1 misdemeanor to use a UAS to violate subsection (a) of the same section, which independently prohibits intentionally interfering with the lawful taking of wildlife resources or driving/harassing/intentionally disturbing wildlife resources for the purpose of disrupting lawful taking (subsection (a) itself, without a UAS, is a Class 2 misdemeanor for a first offense and Class 1 for subsequent offenses). The Wildlife Resources Commission may separately seek civil injunctive relief, including attorney's fees and expert-witness costs.

records.summary: Effective December 1, 2024, Session Law 2024-15 (House Bill 198, enacted after the General Assembly overrode a gubernatorial veto) repealed Article 10 of Chapter 63 of the General Statutes, eliminating the separate North Carolina UAS knowledge test and the State commercial-operator permit requirement (formerly codified at §§ 63-95 and 63-96) that had applied on top of FAA Part 107 certification. As of this repeal, commercial and government UAS operators in North Carolina need only comply with FAA Part 107 (or other applicable federal authorization) and are not required to separately hold a State-issued UAS permit or pass the State knowledge test.

records.regulated_activity: Providing a client with a drone-derived orthomosaic map, 3D digital model, elevation data, distance/volume measurements, or geospatial-metadata-tagged aerial photography -- NCBELS treats this as the unlicensed practice of land surveying if the provider is not a licensed PE/PLS, regardless of whether the provider claims to establish legal boundaries

records.summary: MATERIALLY EXPANDED 2026-08-07: the prior version of this record understated a significant, currently binding risk. NCBELS does not merely lack UAS-specific guidance -- it has actively and repeatedly enforced against small-business drone operators since 2018, issuing cease-and-desist letters to at least a half-dozen companies for practicing land surveying without a license. In the best-documented case, NCBELS investigated and formally warned Michael Jones (360 Virtual Drone Services LLC, Goldsboro, NC) that his orthomosaic mapping, thermal imaging, and geospatial-metadata photography services constituted unlicensed surveying under Chapter 89C, regardless of whether he claimed to establish legal boundaries. Jones sued on First Amendment grounds; the Fourth Circuit ruled for NCBELS on May 20, 2024 (360 Virtual Drone Services LLC v. Ritter, 102 F.4th 263), holding the Board may restrict non-licensees' communication of maps and 3D digital models under a 'loosened' First Amendment standard for occupational speech. The U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari on April 20, 2026, making the Fourth Circuit's ruling final. Per NCBELS's own stated enforcement position (as described in the litigation record), providing a client with any of the following without a PE/PLS license risks unlicensed-practice enforcement: aerial photographs containing geospatial metadata or coordinate/distance information; orthomosaic maps; 3D digital models from photogrammetry; elevation/topographic products; or rough distance or stockpile-volume measurements from processed aerial imagery. Chapter 89C's general competency-in-practice requirement (for licensed PEs/PLS themselves) remains a separate, narrower point within this same statutory framework.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat any UAS-derived deliverable containing geospatial metadata, coordinates, distances, elevations, volumes, or an orthomosaic/3D model as presumptively within NCBELS's asserted licensing scope, per the now-final Fourth Circuit ruling -- route such deliverables through a licensed North Carolina PE or PLS regardless of whether the product purports to establish legal boundaries. Do not assume a disclaimer avoids the licensing requirement; NCBELS's enforcement position does not turn on whether boundary lines are claimed.
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Advise clients that this is an active, currently enforced, and now judicially settled risk in North Carolina -- not a hypothetical gap. Confirm licensure status before a non-licensed operator delivers any mapping/photogrammetry product with the characteristics NCBELS has targeted, and consider the Fourth Circuit's now-final ruling (cert. denied April 2026) when assessing a First Amendment defense, since that avenue is foreclosed in this Circuit.
